Wrote a polished substack version. This is becoming my new workflow. Draft the basic idea here, toss it to ChatGPT to finish for substack.

The Appleby book has me circling a rather delicious thought: AI panic is really cognitive mercantilism. In the book’s account, mercantilism was really 4 beliefs

  1. There’s a fixed amount of wealth in the world in the form of land and species. The goal of politics was to control more land and maintain a positive balance of trade causing bullion accumulation, “beggar thy neighbor” by going “treasure seeking”

  2. Poor people would cause anarchy and societal breakdown if given freedom, and elites had to govern them coercively for their own good

  3. Supply and high prices matter, aggregate demand doesn’t, and the poor in particular are not full economic actors, just factors of production. They eat food and work but the demand side of the economy is for elites and the luxury goods they consume.

  4. It’s no great loss that 80% of humans toil in inefficient agriculture because they’re not good for much else anyway and will just be useless mouths to feed if they don’t labor.

Replace “money” with “intelligence” and you get:

  1. There’s a fixed amount of intelligence in the world in the form of human brains and produced “knowledge species” mined from them. The goal of politics is to gather most of the best brains and maintain positive knowledge trade balance, accumulating knowledge bullion aka “IP”, beggaring neighbors in the knowledge economy, and going “treasure hunting” for intelligence in the form of genius brains and the IP they can produce.

  2. Stupid people need to be governed coercively by cognitive elites for their own good and will cause anarchic breakdown if allowed to think for themselves

  3. Supply control of intelligence and high prices for brains and knowledge species matter, aggregate demand for intelligence doesn’t matter. The stupid in particular are not full cognitive actors, just factors of production. They consume and do limited cognitive labor as work, but demand for intelligence is an elite preserve and for the luxury intelligence goods they consume.

  4. It’s no great loss that 80% of humans toil in inefficient cognition because they’re not good for much else anyway and will just be useless minds to occupy if they don’t labor at whatever they can.

As in the 1600s with rapid improvements in agriculture driving the farming percentage to 5% in a few centuries, improvements in AI mean 80% don’t have to be low-grade intelligence producers. They are far more valuable as intelligence consumers, contributing to limitless aggregate demand for intelligence.

Thanks to those 1600s innovations, I don’t know how to farm but I can have as much food as I want and do other stuff with my energy. And thanks to 2020s innovations I can have as much intelligence as I want and to other things with my attention.

More subtly people voluntarily began working much harder in early capitalism because they wanted more stuff and now had the means to get higher returns on labor to generate the necessary surplus to do so, both on farms and in the new non-farm work. Similarly supposedly “stupid” people, really just lazy thinkers in most cases, now have a reason to think harder because they want more of the products of intelligence and now have the means to get higher returns on attention to generate the necessary surplus to do so.

And extending the same argument to AIs themselves, this is a reason to drive towards full cognitive agency for them, letting them generate demand for intelligence too, not just supply. And AI safety fears are similar to fear of rioting farm laborers.

And notice that just as the elites looked down on trade then (mercantilism was a philosophy not of actual merchants but of militaristic politicians and rentier nobility), they look down on intelligence now. Trump brags ritually about his intelligence but like most political leaders he thinks of the intellectual laboring class as serfs and deploys his own limited intelligence on litigation and extortion. And wants to hoard intelligence like it is bullion.

Capitalism! The new cousin of (Science!) tm.

I started poking around the Kindle sample of the relentless revolution. I am drawn more to the other October Contraptions book club reading, The Birth of the Modern World, but the introduction's definitions* sparked a few ideas.

Specifically the crisp clarity on what constitutes capitalism:

Stated simply, capital becomes capital when someone uses it to gain more money, usually by producing something. We can add an “ism” to “capital” only when the imperatives and strategies of private investments come to dominance as they did first in England and the Netherlands, next in Western Europe, and then in the American colonies.

And what it replaced:

To prevent social unrest, rulers monitored the growing, selling, and exporting of grain crops. Where there were legislatures, they passed restrictive laws. Hemmed in by regulations, people had few opportunities to make trouble—or undertake new enterprises. Most manufacturing went on in the household, where family members turned fibers into fabric and made foodstuffs edible. Custom, not incentives, prompted action and dictated the flow of work throughout the year. People did not assign themselves parts in this social order; tasks were allocated through the inherited statuses of landlord, tenant, father, husband, son, laborer, wife, mother, daughter, and servant.

The folks I know personally (not famous master of the universe types) who are the biggest defenders of capitalism tend to have an atavistic attitude towards preserving the established order. Which is incredibly antithetical to the original impetus and growth of capitalism through risk taking and incentives.

Folks I know who actually use money to gain more money by producting something tend to be more pragmatic. Particularly if they're actually close to producing something and not up in the ether of our abstracted economy.

This reminds me of something VGR said about how Science! (tm) types tend to not be actually interested in the cultural specific behaviors that make up science such as experimentation, testing, predictive power etc. Instead its a rallying cry and political banner. I'd be curious if others have similar experiences and anecdata.

This Capitalism! rather than capitalism framing also helps make sense of the substantial rentseeking we see at the national level. There is increasingly capital invested not in productive enterprises so much as the symbolism of that, larps of doing big important risk taking things rather than actually going forth and boldly building.

There is a lesser mirror of that in state capture locally and in labor union and green economy dynamics where the language of incentives and competition and risk taking is co-opted by cozy interactions between moneyed interests and government power.

On a secant, I find that defintions and introductions can be quite revealing for what they take to be axiomatic. I used to enjoy reading math textbook introductions for exactly that purpose.

“If the causes of the Great Depression elude experts, it's because there are too many of them interacting in hidden ways. This underlines the point that in a free market economy, though some people have much more power than others, no one is in charge.”

Reminds me of the Stevenson Test:

The Stevenson Test

I’ve had a brainworm stuck in my head for a few days, thanks to Sean Stevenson.

Great idea from Sean Stevenson's talk at Protocol Symposium -- the test of New Nature should be that there is nobody to appeal to.

Which sends me back to Paul Ford's cult classic "Why wasn't I consulted" -- the argument that the web is fundamentally a customer service medium, and that WWIC is the fundamental question of the internet, the thing every comment section and pull request and reply-guy is really asking. The two ideas are the same idea from opposite ends: the web was built to make everyone feel consultable, and New Nature is what's left when there's no longer anyone on the other end of the complaint.

This feels like a Turing test type condition for New Nature. Call it the Stevenson test.

We’re familiar with ranting about kafkaesque bureaucracies and hard-coded protocols you can’t argue with. These are appeals to nobody with nowhere to direct them. You could complain online or do standup comedy jokes and hope for some commiseration and laughs.

AI is a new layer of new nature that has created entire new genres of appeals to nowhere/nobody. I don’t know how it’s manifesting irl but online the main genre seems to be poetic copes, often quoting some bit of poignant human artistry with a sentiment like “AI could never do this.”

The interesting thing about such copes is not whether they’re true or false, classy or cringe, or whether others agree. It’s that they’re poetic appeals to nobody, nowhere. And unlike the older layers of new nature marked by hard inflexibility, the AI layer is particularly frustrating because it is so protean and responsive in every other way.

The absent authority you feel you could appeal to feels human shaped. If only an authoritative scientist or even an authoritative AI itself could reassure you that yes, AI cannot do that, it’s mathematically proven.

But there’s nobody listening at the other end. You could complain to a real LLM, and it might even offer reassurance if trained to be kind, but that’s like being handled by the little boy in Waiting for Godot who reassures Vladimir and Estragon that of course Godot will come tomorrow.

Appleby's portrayal of France's forced attempts at capitalism and comparison to England's trial and error makes it clear that you need to let evolutionary forces loose on to a system.

When pushed top-down the substrate, in this case the people, does not change and carries no marks of learning. Whereas if you simply put units of thought in tough positions but with freedom you get as close to the basics of life as you can be and then the natural laws take over.

Reading about the history of European farming and I realize that the show Clarkson’s Farm is less slice of life and more slice of history. Especially since the last few episodes featured the newest farming innovations to increase yield—such as land scanning and targeted manure spreading.

Half-baked thought: When Europe explored the seas and found new Spaces it’s because life and people had already made Places available there.

When we explore the abstract world of knowledge we need to build, create an engine that produces something (if only data), to be able to report back with what we have found.

With global warming, capitalism turns from a force of culture into a force of nature.

Hypothesis: Although nature is slow to enforce the feedback loop through deleterious effects, capitalism can respond fast enough to stymie the worst, as long as culture still has receptors to hear nature.

Appleby almost instantly dunks on Jared Diamond, love it.

“Jared Diamond wrote a best-selling study that emphasized the geographic and biological advantages the West enjoyed. Two central problems vexed this interpretation: The advantages of the West are enjoyed by all of Europe, but only England experience the breakthroughs that others had to imitate to become capitalistic”

Joyce Appleby — The Relentless Revolution audio/video links

1. New Books Network — The Relentless Revolution

Open-web episode page

A 57-minute interview with Joyce Appleby, hosted by Marshall Poe, devoted directly to The Relentless Revolution: A History of Capitalism. This is the best place to start because Appleby explains her central argument that capitalism was a historically specific development rather than the inevitable expression of a timeless human instinct to trade.

2. New Books in Economic and Business History — Apple Podcasts

Apple Podcasts show page

This is the Apple Podcasts channel for the New Books Network's economic and business-history interviews. The Apple catalogue doesn't currently expose a stable direct link to the old Appleby episode, so search “Joyce Appleby” within the show; the open-web link above is easier for this particular episode.

3. ALOUD / Los Angeles Public Library — What's the Matter with Capitalism?

Listen on the LAPL website

This 1-hour 13-minute conversation pairs Appleby with entrepreneur and writer Peter Barnes to discuss whether capitalism can reconcile private interests with the public good. It isn't simply a summary of Relentless Revolution; it takes the historical framework of the book and pushes it toward questions about what capitalism might look like in the twenty-first century.

4. C-SPAN Q&A — Joyce Appleby

C-SPAN — Q&A with Joyce Appleby

Brian Lamb's May 16, 2010 Q&A with Appleby features an extended discussion of The Relentless Revolution. It's technically a television interview rather than a podcast, but it's long-form and works very well as an audio listen if you want Appleby to elaborate on the intellectual background and arguments of the book.

5. Reason TV — The Relentless Revolution: Joyce Appleby on the History of Capitalism

Watch/listen on Reason

This is a much shorter ~8-minute interview with Appleby focused on capitalism's historical role in generating wealth and how it compares with competing economic systems. It's useful as a compact distillation of a few of the book's big claims, but substantially less nuanced than the New Books or ALOUD conversations.

6. Crash Course — Capitalism and Socialism: World History #33

Apple Podcasts episode

John Green gives an 18-minute overview of the emergence of industrial capitalism and socialism, and the episode explicitly lists Appleby's The Relentless Revolution among its sources. It's not an interview with Appleby and doesn't engage her thesis in depth, but it's a useful quick historical scaffold before or alongside the book.
